utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you. And good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Before we start with the examination of the next witness, the Chamber would like to hear the Defence's position on the report of Mr. Dunjic, which we discussed last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence will be utilizing Dr. Stankovic to defend the report with his supplements or additions to the same, primarily matters that he can confirm and have the same opinion as in the report, or where his opinion may be more extensive or differ would be the subject of a short supplement to that report or notations in relation to paragraphs of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, another matter is how much time Mr. Stankovic would need to prepare his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The materials have been given to him and the preliminary estimate is that he believes by some time in the first part of January he should be able to have it all done with the -- any supplement thereto. But that's a very preliminary estimate since, again, he has just received the materials recently and I don't know how extensive of a review is required, but we will update if any new information comes to our attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And is it your intention that then a new supplementary report will be produced or just that Mr. Stankovic will prepare for, if I could say so, defending? That means being cross-examined on the expert report of Mr. Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I think any work product of Mr. Stankovic, whatever form it takes, would qualify as an expert report if it is any material that is not contained in the Dunjic or different from the Dunjic or expanding on the Dunjic. And I don't know if we could deal with that as a proofing matter or as a completely new report since it's relating to the existing report that has already gone through the 94 bis process. So I'm kind of not -- not quite in a position yet to know without seeing how substantive any additional supplement would be to qualify it as a new report or simply a matter of proofing on the existing report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, one of the options also considered by you, if I understand you well, was just to accept the report, not necessarily the content of it, and refrain from asking the expert to be called to be cross-examined. Have you considered that? Because that would change the situation a bit for the Defence. I think that was one of the options considered when we dealt with the matter last time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, I also recall that was one of the options that was raised in court and that Mr. McCloskey indicated he would consider. I think we were waiting for the Defence response before coming to a final view. And I will double-check with Mr. McCloskey, but I think for various reasons we began looking skeptically at that option and considered that the most prudent course would be the allowance for a certain level of examination, depending on what was submitted. So probably -- and those discussions were taking place with some intensity between Mr. McCloskey and other members of the team directly concerned with the Dunjic report. I can check quickly to see if what I have related is fully accurate and get back to the Court at the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please do that. Because it sounds as if that option, report is there, no need to call anyone for -- to be cross-examined or on -- on that report. Of course, it could not be Mr. Dunjic but also not Mr. Stankovic, whether that option is now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I can certainly appreciate that the Court would like to know where it stands and I'll get back immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you very much. Mr. Ivetic, perhaps it's best to wait for the final position of the Defence. Then before we start with the -- yes, Prosecution. Then before we start with the next witness, I'd like to briefly deal with the associated exhibits related to this witness. Pursuant to its Rule 92 ter motion for Witness Akashi, dated the 27th of October, 2015, and most recent exhibit list received on the 20th of November, the Defence has tendered 37 associated exhibits. The Chamber notes that three of these have already been admitted into evidence, leaving 34. The Chamber reiterates to the Defence its guidance that the Chamber should not be flooded with associated exhibits, and the Chamber also recalls the preference for documents to be tendered during the witness's examination in court which allow the witness to explain and comment on them. The Chamber therefore invites the Defence to reduce the number of associated exhibits it is tendering through this witness. Alternatively, could the Defence explain why these documents need to be tendered as associated exhibits, as opposed to being tendered during the examination-in-chief of this witness? Mr. Ivetic, there's a clear invitation here. Of course, we do not know, also in view of the time you have asked for examination-in-chief, how much of these associated exhibits you'd like to touch upon during your examination, but if there's any observation you'd like to make you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I note some of the associated exhibits are rather lengthy. I will be dealing with the lengthy ones in court so we'll only be dealing with parts of those exhibits which will be presented to the witness and which then we will not need to have introduced since they'll be read into the record. So I will try to limit the number of lengthy exhibits that come in. It's still likely to be a large number because there are a lot of small, one- or two-page documents that were used with the witness in parts of his testimony from the Karadzic case. I can perhaps reassess at the conclusion of the evidence which of those I might be able to exclude. Of course, some of them relate to the Prosecution's cross-examination during the Karadzic case so I feel if I try to exclude any of those, then I could be accused of not giving a full picture of the testimony. So I'm hesitant to do that. But will I try to see if I can shorten things as far as exhibits are concerned after the conclusion of all aspects of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course, this Chamber doesn't know anything about the cross-examination of this witness in Karadzic. We haven't -- it has not been tendered, it has not been presented to us. And usually the --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is a part of the Rule 92 ter statement, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. Then I thought I read some 90 or 95 pages of transcript. I saw here and there Ms. Edgerton dealing with some matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then I could be mistaken. In any event, I think I will deal with the associated exhibits at the very end after we finish the witness so we'll have time to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just a couple of matters. I don't believe that cross-examination was included.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I then express my surprise, Mr. Ivetic, that where I having read the 90 pages over the weekend and having no recollection as to what was tendered, that you apparently think that cross-examination is part of that. I saw that Ms. Edgerton has intervened a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. -- I didn't mean to interrupt, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was only going to respond to the other matters raised by Mr. Ivetic and indicate that I appreciate and I am confident he will do his best to follow the Court's guidance. In support of that effort I'd simply note that it was my impression from working with these materials that they were -- these were matters all raised in the examination, discussed at some point during the examination, and it seemed to me that it might indeed be the most efficient way of proceeding. Otherwise we'll have two discussions of those -- of many of those documents in court - the one in the transcript from the Karadzic case that's been submitted and the one that Mr. Ivetic might be attempting to elicit in response to the Court's guidance. So, in that sense, I would, I suppose, support the exceptional request to -- that identifies as -- this many documents as associated. In any event, we'll both have to consider I think at some point which of the documents that seem, if any, that seem to have been associated or considered to have been associated by the parties up to this moment or not and possibly adjust our examinations accordingly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tieger. I still do not see any cross-examination in the materials. I think it finished on one day and then there was a little bit remaining for the next day. And then on that next day, I think the accused then concluded his examination-in-chief and -- I have not seen any cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You are correct, Your Honours. I apologise. I stand corrected. I, of course, did read the whole thing in preparation for the witness and [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that. You may not have been aware. At the same time, I think it's important to know what exactly was presented to this Chamber and what was not. Then, I think it's time to ask the usher to escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Akashi.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, I have addressed you as Mr. Akashi. I have read that in other -- before other Chambers often you were addressed as Your Excellency. It's not any way as a depreciation of your titles and your -- the honours that have been given to you, but it's just this Chamber has developed a habit in just addressing everyone as Mr. or Mrs. Please don't misunderstand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You're most gracious and I fully understand. I think titles have only the effect of inflating some people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether I would support that. But, Mr. Akashi, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to first ask to you please state your full name for the purposes of the record.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, my full name is Yasushi Akashi.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I would ask for 1D5815 to be displayed in e-court. I do have a hard copy for the ambassador of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Ambassador, while we wait for the same I can ask you a question. Did you have occasion to testify in the case at this Tribunal in relation to Radovan Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, then you'll certainly have read again that you were asked at that time whether you had any papers before you. If you want to consult anything other than the hard copy of the testimony in the Karadzic case, would you please tell us that you are doing it and what you are consulting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I will follow your instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, this document before us in e-court is the transcript from the Karadzic proceeding dated 24 April 2013. Does that accord with your recollection of the first day you started to testify in direct examination in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if now we could turn briefly to page 79 of the document, and it will be tabbed in the hard copy at the top for your convenience, here on the screen we now see the transcript from the same case, dated 25 April 2013. Sir, does that accord with your recollection of the second day that you testified in direct examination in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, this seem to be the -- in accordance with what I said on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And, sir, did you have occasion to review this transcript from the Karadzic case in these last few days before today?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I cannot say I went through every word of it, but this seems to be in general accord with what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And after the -- after your review, do you think the transcript is accurate and complete as to the testimony that you gave in the direct examination in the Karadzic case?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if I were to ask you today questions exactly the same as those in the Karadzic transcript, would your answers today be in substance the same as in this transcript?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I hope so. But you said in substance, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you have taken a solemn declaration to tell the truth today. Can you tell us if your answers in the Karadzic case were truthful in nature as recorded?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: As I saw the events in those days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would thus tender 1D5815 as a public exhibit. And as we indicated, we would deal with the associated exhibits after the conclusion of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I hear of no objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1361, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1361 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. At this time I have a short public summary of the transcript for the public to know some of the matters that were testified about, a copy of which has been given to the booths.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Have you informed Mr. Akashi about the purpose of this summary?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I can repeat again --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, this is a short summary just for purposes of the public. It is does not form part of your evidence. Your transcript is your evidence.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador Akashi joined the UN in February of 1957. He served from then on in a variety of offices and functions in his career, ranging from ambassador to under-secretary-general, until he retired from the UN in 1997. In 1992, Ambassador Akashi was appointed the Special Representative of the Secretary-General of the UN for the former Yugoslavia and served in that capacity during the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina. After retiring from the UN he went back to Japan. In his transcript from the Karadzic case, Ambassador Akashi testifies as to a number of matters including, but not limited to, the following. He says the basic trouble --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Ivetic. I think there's an error here. In 1992 I was appointed the Special Representative of the Secretary-General of the UN for Cambodia. And it was in January 1994 that I was appointed on the same -- the same, similar job with regard to former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree with that and I misspoke. And I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador Akashi says the basic trouble with UNPROFOR in former Yugoslavia was a lack of unity of opinion within the Security Council where at least three differing viewpoints prevailed. This made the work of UNPROFOR difficult. There was no peace to keep in the former Yugoslavia, and the UN Secretary-General and others had serious doubts about the UN going there, but European countries exerted pressure on the UN to step in. Governments were in many ways compelled to do something to respond to the voices of public opinion and media cries. Some UNPROFOR officers, such as General Briquemont, felt the mandate given to the peacekeepers was extremely ambiguous and almost impossible to implement. Demilitarization of the safe areas, including Srebrenica, was a constant issue raised, and it was repeatedly pointed out that the lack of demilitarization affected an indispensable element of the safe area concept itself. Many reports to the Security Council reported problems as to all the safe areas. As to six safe areas, the problems included several defects or shortcomings in both the concept and implementation of the safe areas, which led the Secretary-General and others to have serious reservations and express their concerns. First, only less than a quarter of requested UN troops to implement the agreements were provided. Second --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but this typewritten version seems not in perfect accord with the original text. There were some slips.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the final transcript usually gets combed and those typos get fixed.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Okay, fine. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, what is written now will be reviewed before it becomes the final transcript. And there is an audio available to check whether everything is okay. And that's usually done the same day or the same night.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your reassurance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Second, the Bosnian side used the safe areas to rest and re-equip their troops and other purposes. Third, the disarmament provisions were not implemented. Fourth, there was not always demarcation of the safe areas. Ambassador Akashi agreed with observations of others that premature recognition of Croatia and Bosnia worsened the situation. European governments should have heeded the advice of Badinter Commission of the EU to make sure first the constitutions of Bosnia and Croatia provided for the vital interests of both majority and minority groups. At one point in time, the main -- an issue was that neither the Bosnian government nor the United States government wanted a long-term cease-fire because of concerns of making territorial holdings of the Serb forces permanent. As a result of active military assistance from the United States, Germany, and the Islamic states to Croatian and Bosnian forces, the overall power balance drastically shifted against the Serb side as the war progressed. It was the UN's consistent position that if there were infractions by any side, that the use of air power was to be applied equally to the parties. But this position was not shared by NATO or some governments. As to the Markale 1 shelling, the Ambassador appointed a commission of experts that determined the attack could have come from either side. And that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, I would now propose to return to parts of your transcript from the Karadzic proceedings to ask you some questions to clarify and seek further information.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could thus have D1361 on our screens, and page 5 of the same, which should correlate to transcript page 37667 of the underlying transcript. And, sir, here at lines 10 through 12, you say and I quote: "The basic trouble with UNPROFOR in the former Yugoslavia was lack of unity of opinions or viewpoints in the Security Council." You then in the remainder of this answer through line 19 say that at least three different viewpoints prevailed among the permanent members of the Security Council. What were these three different viewpoints?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: One was the viewpoint of the United States that the Bosnian government was basically the victim of the aggression by Bosnian Serb forces supported by Serbia. And second viewpoint was that of the Russian Federation which considered the -- the Bosnian Serbs as a minority group which was defending its rights against the majority group, which was the Bosnian government. The third viewpoint was held by countries like the United Kingdom and France which felt that the most important thing to do is to stabilize the situation, not the designation of who was the main culprit of the difficulties, and that some kind of peace and the cessation of hostilities was the main objective of the international community. Of course, German position was somewhat different, somewhere between, you might say, the position of the United States and that of the French and the British. And many Islamic countries who were non-permanent members of the Security Council were anxious that the injustice, as they saw it, suffered by the Bosnian government should be corrected. So these were three or you might say four different viewpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Next I'd like to turn to page 8 which should correlate to transcript page 37607 of the underlying Karadzic transcript, and here first I'd like to focus at lines 15 through 25 on this page. And here, you again discuss the Security Council compromises that led to ambiguity in resolutions which were difficult to understand and difficult to implement on the ground. Did anyone from the ground ever tell the Security Council of these problems that were being experienced by those trying to implement their resolutions?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think many of us did that, within the limit of basic politeness which we always adhered to, vis-à-vis members of the Security Council, and including the Secretary-General himself. His reports pointed out the difficulty of implementing Security Council resolutions which did their best to hide the differences among Security Council members and tried to paper over these differences with the use of ambiguous and seemingly elegant phraseology.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now, sir, looking at the earlier part of this same page, more specifically your answer at lines -- beginning at lines 4 through 14, here you talk of the media and how governments were compelled to do something to respond to public opinion and calls from the media. Was the media presenting a full and accurate picture of what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think to generalise the media would not be doing justice to the media. There was a big variation about the accuracy of the -- or balance of the media coverage. For instance, if you take up only television media, I think, on the whole, BBC was more accurate and more balanced than CNN, for instance. Some are more emotional than others, and -- so -- but I think there was a proclivity on the part of commercial media to sensationalise issues and to simplify the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And next I would turn to page 34 of the transcript, which is the underlying page 37696, and here if we could focus on lines 11 through 16, your answer here talks about the topic that you just raised, the media that sometimes "tended to exaggerate the nature of incidents so they can sort of sensationalise their nature." Do you recall any specific examples of this that related to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I cannot offhand recall specific instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then if we can turn to page 11 in e-court and that will be transcript page 37673 of the underlying transcript, and here the question posed from you is at lines 4 through 9 and it deals with the part of your -- where your book where you say that neither the Bosnian government nor United States government wanted a long-term cease-fire based on the view of not wanting Serb territorial holdings to be permanent. Then at lines 15 through 17, you are asked, in essence, if this selection from your book refreshes your recollection on different interests of foreign elements and domestic elements prolonging the war. And then on the next page at line 3 we finally get your answer to these questions, which is recorded as: "Yes, that was my interpretation of events at that time." Do you recall any specific matters or events that brought you to that interpretation?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I negotiated in Geneva, I think it was in June 1994, so could -- we had heard proximity talks between three parties in the Bosnian conflict, Bosnian Serbs, Bosnian government, and the Croat -- Bosnian Croats. And since they did not want to meet face to face with two others, the -- I had to go through different rooms where three parties were ensconced. And the -- I was able to extract a commitment on the part of Bosnian Serbs to agree to at least a four-month cease-fire proposed by the UN and they did agree to it. But Bosnian government did not want to accept cease-fire as being too long, and this coincided with the American viewpoint presented by Ambassador Redman that cease-fire period should be for one month. And Croats were somewhere in a position vacillating between these different periods.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And further down on the page from line 11 through 23 you talk about a visit of President Carter to Bosnia, and in lines 16 through 17 you say: "But Bosnian government did not particularly appreciate Carter's visit." Could you please explain for us what this relates to?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yeah, I was negotiating at the time towards the end of 1994 as general cessation of hostilities agreement between the three parties, and I found the Bosnian government reluctant to accept the four-month period. I think Serbs were somewhat more willing to do it, and the Croats, as usual, vacillated between two other positions. And -- but in the end I was able to extract agreement among the three parties for a general cessation of hostilities agreement for a four-month period. And President Carter helped me with regard to getting agreement of Bosnian Serbs which were, I think, any way forthcoming. So I -- like what media said, I'm not sure how much President Carter's help was actually needed. It was obvious that Bosnian government was not happy with that visit by President Carter, and yet I think the coincidence of interests by the three parties enabled us to get four month's cessation of hostilities. But at the end of that, hostilities again were rekindled.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to turn together with you to page 24 in e-court which should correlate to transcript page 37686 of the underlying transcript. And at lines 5 through 8 as your answer, you say: "Yes. Demilitarization of safe areas, including Srebrenica, was one of our preoccupations, and we never stopped pointing out that the lack of demilitarization of safe areas is an indispensable component of the safe area concept itself." First of all, do you mean to say that the lack of demilitarization of safe areas is an indispensable component of the safe areas concept or do you mean to say demilitarization is an indispensable component of the safe areas concept?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Demilitarization of the safe areas was very important and as you quoted in -- even indispensable part of safety and security of safe areas. But as I said elsewhere, other elements like delimitation or delineation of the scope of respective safe areas was also important, and the freedom of movement by UNPROFOR and others was also important. In addition, the very presence of the UN to supervise the safe areas was also important. Here, if our presence was just symbolic, then that would not be sufficient to ensure safety and security of these areas. So these three or four different elements were interlocking assurances for the effectiveness of safe areas. But I must add that in the case of Srebrenica and Zepa, the delineation and demilitarization at one period or the other, I think in initial period was partly achieved and then somehow they deteriorated.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in this part of the transcript you say "we never stopped pointing out." To whom was this that you never stopped pointing out this problem?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Primarily to the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, what did the Security Council do, if anything, in response?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I regret to say that, as I said earlier, the lack of unity of its members, including the permanent members, was characteristic of the Security Council in the whole Yugoslav episode. This is in sharp contrast to the effectiveness of the Security Council and its unity during the Cambodian conflict in which there was a remarkable degree of unity of approach as well as attitude. And so you might say this is a fundamental underlying necessity for the effectiveness of the UN, that its members, particularly permanent members, be united in the basic objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to demilitarization, was that also raised with the Bosnian government?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, all these matters were raised with the Bosnian government, as well as with the Bosnian Serb party.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And as to demilitarization what was their response?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Bosnian government insisted that their military forces had to remain, particularly with regard to Sarajevo they emphasised. You know, it was a seat of the government and therefore they needed military presence sufficient to enable the tranquility and safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to page 49 in e-court of the transcript and that should correlate to 37711 of the underlying Karadzic transcript. At lines 7 through 15 of the same, you were asked a question by Mr. Karadzic and it goes as follows: "Do you remember -- do you remember our meeting on 22nd of April, 1994, in Belgrade, where I claim that the BH army launching attacks from the safe areas and that I seeked and requested the UN to proceed immediately to Gorazde to be able to accurately report who was attacking?" "A. I think in our meeting on the 22nd of April, 1994, we discussed many things. That meeting started at 12.00 noon and went on until 11.30 that night. So it was a marathon negotiation. We discussed many, many things centring, of course, around Gorazde crisis." Ambassador, was one of the things discussed during that marathon negotiation these matters that were raised by Mr. Karadzic in his question?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Could you repeat what Karadzic raised at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He raised -- he claimed that the BH army was launching attacks from safe areas and that he requested the UN to proceed to Gorazde to be able to accurately report who was attacking. That's his question, and I'm asking if you recall if that specific item was one of the items that would have been discussed at that marathon negotiation.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I -- I do not specifically remember reference to this matter, but I hasten to add that we had a small UN presence in the form of the UNMOs, military observers. I think they numbered eight. And what Karadzic was asking is not a UN presence but a more numerous UN presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I understand. And now if we can turn to the next page in e-court which will correspond to page 37712 of the underlying Karadzic transcript, and at lines 17 through 22 you are giving an answer and you say that -- you talk of many reports of the Secretary-General to the Security Council as to these problems. And this is in reference to Karadzic's question about paragraph 3 of the document you were looking at. So I'd like to look at that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that is number -- 65 ter number 16806. And I also have a hard copy of the same to provide to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, may I draw to your attention that the last answer, that the whole last line has not been translated and transcribed because you immediately started your next question not waiting for the finalization of the translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Then. Perhaps to be on the safe side I should ask the ambassador --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will be worked over -- I mean, overnight. That's not the problem, but then we have to wait until tomorrow, I think. The witness said that it was not about the presence but about increasing the number of those present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But I leave it our transcribers to finalize it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now that we have this document in front of us, we see it is dated the 23rd of April, 1994, and references a meeting with Bosnian Serb civilian and military leaders. If we could turn to page 2 of the same and look at the paragraph 3 that Mr. Karadzic was basing his question on, and it says: "In view of the importance and urgency to reach a concrete agreement on the Gorazde crisis, Mr. Akashi suggested that this item be addressed first. Dr. Karadzic, in addressing the issue, said that the fundamental problem of the safe areas was that they did not meet the criteria of safe areas as defined in international conventions. Of the six designated safe areas only two - Srebrenica and Zepa - had been delineated but still remained undemilitarized. The others served as strongholds for the BiH armija. Consequently there was a need to solve not only the issue of Gorazde but the status of other safe areas as well." Now, in the transcript you say -- strike that. Did the reports of the Secretary-General to the Security Council about these problem -- include anything about these problems?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. When we were looking at the transcript we talked about reports to the Security Council on the topic of safe areas. Did those reports also encompass these that have been raised in this document as expressed by the Serb side, by Dr. Karadzic in particular?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: There were several reports of the UN Secretary-General referring to the questions of difficulties encountered by the UN in order to implement the safe area concept. And so maybe there are slight differences in the way the matter was described or analysed, but in the basic line Secretary-General's approach was the same and consistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I see we're at the time for a break. I would at this time tender this document as the next exhibit. Then we can take that break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 16806 will be Exhibit D1362, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1362 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Akashi, we'll take a break. We'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, the Chamber was informed that you wanted to raise a matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I indicated to the Court I wanted to get back to you as quickly as possible and -- in response to your inquiry earlier today. And that's why I've asked for this brief time. I wanted to advise you that Mr. McCloskey's initial response to the possibility of the simple tendering of the report with nothing else was apparently predicated on his understanding that it had either been proposed by the Defence or that the Defence did not object. Our current understanding, however, is that the Defence does object, and in light of that we do not consider that the preferable option but instead consider that a targeted, short, proofing note-style contribution by Dr. Stankovic would be the more suitable option.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, you can confirm that that option was not accepted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While most of the discussions were between Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Lukic, the part I was there for talked about potentially submitting the transcripts of the cross-examination in the prior proceeding which we felt then would unfairly prejudice us if we did not have a chance to, in essence, re-direct an expert on those topics. But again, most of the discussions were between Mr. Lukic and Mr. McCloskey directly without my involvement. I was only there for a part of the discussions last week, I believe it was Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So then as matters stand now, unless there's any change in the positions is that we'll -- that the Dunjic report will be added to by Mr. Stankovic and that Mr. Stankovic will be called to be briefly examined and be cross-examined. That's -- unless we hear otherwise from the parties, that's what the Chamber now understands the case to be. Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom again. Meanwhile I used the time for P7681. On the 19th of November of this year, during the testimony of Mitar Kovac, Exhibit P7681, a military report, was admitted into evidence. To be found on transcript page 41640. The Chamber notes that the original has a stamp in the upper left-hand corner with the date the 11th of April, 1993. However, in the English translation, the date is 11 April 1992. The Chamber hereby requests the Prosecution to verify and correct the translation. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the transcript, line 8, on page 25 should read "11 April" instead of "1 April."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If we can call up again the transcript of the Karadzic case, which is D1361, and if we could turn to page 74 in e-court which should correlate to page 37736 of the underlying transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, here, you are talking about the Secretary-General's reservations about the concept of safe areas. And in lines 2 through 21 on the page, you outline some of the problems raised by the Secretary-General in more detail. At lines 13 through 14, you say the "UN Security Council in its wisdom did not heed very much to these opinions of the Secretary-General," as to the safe areas. To your knowledge, was there a particular member or members of the Security Council that had views in relation to addressing these problems that were listed here in your answer?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not quite understand your question, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In relation to the problems that are raised here in your testimony that the Secretary-General addressed to the Security Council, do you recall if there was any discussion within the Security Council as to those problems?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There was a prolonged and repeated discussions in the Security Council with the participation of all its members.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And in the end, was there a particular position that prevailed within the Security Council in relation to these problems?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And you said a little bit before the break that in relation to disarmament, after some initial success the situation deteriorated. Were there any indications that more weapons were being brought into the safe areas after they'd been declared?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: It's difficult to generalise because there was six safe areas and situation differed from one area to another. And in the question which we were discussing just before the recess, it was the -- the most urgent issue was connected with the Gorazde safe area. So it varied from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can turn to 1D4661 in e-court, and I have a hard copy of that document as well for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is a document that was discussed with you within the Karadzic transcript at pages 37727 through 37729. And you can perhaps see from the copy on the screen and soon in the hard copy that will be given to you that this is dated -- first of all, it's from General de Lapresle to Mr. Annan dated 14 February 1995 with the subject: "Unidentified fixed-wing aircraft flights in Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the next page in both the hard copy and in e-court, I propose to discuss ... I see counsel on his feet. I don't know if there's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, just in respect of the hard copy, it may be that you only wish to present this portion of the document. There's just a -- and it's only a tiny portion of the document that appears to me to be missing and it's point 9 and then in the back of that is a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct. I inadvertently left those off. I just saw that but I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that you'll provide them now --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can provide them. I will not be asking questions about that section, but if you want the -- in fairness the whole idea of having a hard copy is to give the complete document to the gentleman, so I should provide them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could I meanwhile, before Mr. Akashi focuses on the next question, ask one thing. Mr. Akashi, you answered one of the previous questions by saying it's difficult to generalise because there were six safe areas and the situation differed from one area to another. And then you said: "And in the question we were discussing just before the recess, it was the -- the most urgent issue was connected with the Gorazde safe area." And you said it varied from time to time. I remember that Mr. Ivetic in his question referred to a situation deteriorating as far as demilitarization is concerned. Now what I read from your testimony from before the break, and I'll read that part of your answer. You said: "But I must add that in the case of Srebrenica and Zepa, the delineation and demilitarization at one period or the other, I think an initial period was partly achieved and then somehow they deteriorated." So I wondered whether Mr. Ivetic's question was about that portion of your evidence. It was. And I'm slightly confused that in your answer now you are referring to Gorazde, whereas in that portion of your answer before the break you referred to Srebrenica and Zepa where it deteriorated over time. Could you help me out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think we were paying attention to different periods. I think when I talked about temporary improvements of the situation with regard to Srebrenica and Zepa, Srebrenica safe area was the first of the six to be established, and in the initial period, delineation and disarmament part went rather well in Srebrenica, in particular. This was a local agreement, not of general application to all safe areas. Anyway, the other areas came into existence at a somewhat later period. But in the initial period, there were ups and downs, and there were short periods of some optimism on the local situation, particularly in Srebrenica. But then there was a focus of worldwide attention after the Markale market situation in Sarajevo in February 1994, and the attention shifted to Gorazde in April 1994. And in those areas there were certainly no demarcation of boundaries, nor any substantive disarmament efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I just -- one follow-up question. You said and the attention shifted to Gorazde and in those areas there were certainly demarcation of boundaries or no demarcation of boundaries? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here again, difficult to generalise, but there were general difficulties of demarcation, and I think the cases of Sarajevo and Zepa were rather specific and temporary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My question was only about what -- the last sentence you said. Because in my view there was a "no" missing in the transcript. I read in the transcript: "... there were certainly demarcation of boundaries, nor" and then it went on. Were there demarcation or no demarcation of boundaries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the majority of the cases, no demarcation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, if I could draw your attention to item number 7 on the document that we have before us which reads: "We are not yet in a position to comment in detail on these events, but it appears that two clandestine resupplies have taken place. The equipment being delivered is assessed to be of a high value/high technology such as new generation antitank guided missiles or perhaps surface to air missiles. Regardless it is unreasonable to expect that just two aircraft deliveries could provide enough supplies required for the BiH forces, and that more resupply flights are likely. The origin of the cargo aircraft or the jet [sic] is not known." And in relation to this document, if we could look at the transcript for the Karadzic case, D1361, page 65 of the same in e-court and that will be page 37727, lines 10 through 12. You say in relation to this: "1995. I do not specifically recall an incident in February 1995 with regard to Tuzla airport. The incidents at or around Tuzla were very frequent." And I wanted to, first of all, ask you: Does your answer about incidents being very frequent relate to incidents of the type that we just looked at or in general?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes. In relation to here where you say, "The incidents at or around Tuzla were very frequent," when talking about incidents are you only talking about the type that we just looked at and which was then shown to you in this same transcript, dated from February 1995? What is it that you're talking about when you say "incidents"? That's basically the question.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Throughout the two years, 1994 to 1995, particularly in 1994, the question of the opening of the Tuzla airport for the freedom of movement, particularly to facilitate movement of humanitarian goods, was very much on my agenda. But I -- I think this report you mentioned stemmed from one incident which occurred in February 1995, and I do not have specific recollection of that incident. I think it was dealt with at the military level rather than at the political, diplomatic level.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Mladic, apart from speaking aloud a minute ago, would you please draw your attention to what happens here in the court rather than to communicate in a way, as you know, you're not allowed with the public gallery. So if you turn a little bit, then it will be better visible for us that you're focusing on what happens here rather than to deal with other matters. I invited you to slightly turn, Mr. Mladic, away from the public gallery. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Ambassador, in February of 1995, were there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, the first thing you now do is again turn to the public gallery which I just told you not to do. This is the last warning. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In February 1995, were there restrictions in place on the use of the air-space over Bosnia-Herzegovina; that is, the operation of aircraft by the warring parties? Do you recall? Ambassador, do you recall if there any restrictions on the use of aircraft in the air-space above Bosnia in February of 1995?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I -- I remember there was general restriction.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you recall if during this period there were any restrictions in place in regard to providing weapons to any of the warring parties?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would tender 1D4661 as a Defence exhibit at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D1363, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1363 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I'd like to look at page 25 of the transcript in e-court, which will be 37687 of the underlying transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at lines 17 through 25, and it goes onto the next page, you talk about the expert committee that was established to investigate the first Markale market shelling. And here you say, at line 21 and onward, that two members each were picked from countries friendly to each of the parties. Do you recall the way this alignment worked, who was considered to be members of the commission that would be from countries that were friendly towards either of the sides?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think this committee consisted of five members, and two of them came from countries with some favourable attitude towards Bosnian Serb party and two others from Islamic countries. And the fifth member who served as the chairman was from Canada, which in my opinion was considered neutral and impartial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could turn to page 26 in e-court, which is the very next page of the transcript, in the continuation of your testimony about this committee, you talk of the conclusion reached by the experts, which you accepted fully, was the attack could have come from either side. Did you have faith in these experts and the conclusion that they reached?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: So far as, yeah, they were able to reach their conclusions, I think this is expert view. And -- but that was a rather general conclusion in character under the circumstances because there was only one mortar bomb, and the crater created by the result of the bombing was not very precise due to the fact that the bomb fell not directly on the ground but it encountered some object in the market on the way to finding its place on the ground. So it was not extremely precise or conclusive. And the general conclusion reached by the expert committee was that in view of the general angle and the estimated distance between the Markale market and the place where the mortar was issued, there were in the general areas partly occupied by the Bosnian Serb party and partly occupied by the Bosnian government side, so their conclusion was that the mortar could have come from either one of the two parties. This is quite contrary to the press reports which had appeared in the "New York Times" and others that it came from one party or another. But you know, under the circumstances, we have to rely on the expert opinion however inconclusive it might be.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could next turn to page 31 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: These experts who constituted this five-member committee, were they experts in mortar investigations or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sir, they were experts in ballistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Ballistics. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could now turn page 31 of this same transcript, which should correlate to page 37693 of the underlying Karadzic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Here, on lines 16 and onward, you were asked about the weapons exclusion zone in Sarajevo and weapon collection points. And here, from line 21 onwards to 25, you say that UNPROFOR would have an intermediary presence between the opposing forces. Did the intermediary presence of UNPROFOR, was that allowed in every instance; that is to say, did it work as planned? Did the parties permit the intermediary presence of UNPROFOR in every instance?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: So far as I recollect, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic, no speaking aloud.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm told that the Serbian translation stopped.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If that's the case that will be repaired. Let's wait for a second. By the way, whispering to Mr. Stojanovic's ears would do the same instead of speaking aloud. But could you confirm, Mr. Stojanovic, that the B/C/S translation is now accurate again.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I confirm that we hear now this B/C/S translation, but we did not hear either the previous question or the previous answer. That's what the General was saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then -- what's your suggestion, we could re-read it, which may be the best. Mr. Stojanovic, if you could assist in telling us from where -- is it from: "Here, on lines 16 and onward"?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's from the question asked by Mr. Ivetic and I believe it is from line 17 on page 34.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in 17 Mr. Ivetic says that he has been told that the Serbian translation stopped so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think it must be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it line 8? Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It must be. I don't have any means of verifying, of course, since I was listening to the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's -- I'll read, then, from line 8. The question was: "Here, on lines 16 and onwards, you were asked about the weapons," I take it, "exclusion zone in Sarajevo and weapon collection points. And here, from line 21 onwards to 25, you say that UNPROFOR would have an intermediary presence between the opposing forces. Did the intermediary presence of UNPROFOR, was that allowed in every instance; that is to say, did it work as planned?" And then I take it, "did the parties permit the intermediary presence of UNPROFOR in every instance?" And the answer given then by the witness was: "So far as I recollect, yes." Does that complete, Mr. Stojanovic, the lacking translation? If so, we'll proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it does, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then if we could turn the page to the next page of the Karadzic transcript, which will then be 37694 of the underlying Karadzic transcript, and in this section at line 19 and onwards at the bottom of the page, you were discussing a document identified as a protocol that talked about the right to self-defence and the -- in the event of withdrawal of the interposition of UNPROFOR from the interposition area or if UNPROFOR is not able to prevent or stop attacks. I wish to look at that document with you and that is D112 in the Mladic case, and I do have a hard copy of that as well. Hopefully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Usher, could you ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that hard copy, you can see on the screen that this is dated 16 August 1994. And it's from yourself to Mr. Annan and others in New York and it's entitled: "Weapon collection points." And in relation to the same, if we look at item number 2, it says: "The recent fighting around Visoko-Olovo-Kladanj could pose a complex and dangerous situation whereby a BiH offensive seriously threatens the BSA forces in that area, which is in very close proximity to the northern edge of the Sarajevo EZ. BiH action may be in the form of a provocation or a real desire for tactical gain. Should the BiH move heavy weapons into the zone, this would put them in clear violation of the EZ. In recent days, the BiH have also fired weapons already within the zone. BiH activity has already prompted the BSA to seek to withdraw their heavy weapons from the WCPs." And if we could turn the page and look at, first, items 3 and 5, 3 talks of "the protocol to the Sarajevo WCP agreement of 14 February 1994 (attached) recognises the BSA's legitimate right of self-defence. If the BSA comes under more pressure from the BiH, their demand to have access to their weapons could become a more pressing reality under the protocol referred to above. There are several scenarios that could prevail, and the staff at BH command and UNPROFOR HQ are examining these." And in item 5: "This problem is now being examined in detail. It raises many questions including the numbers and types of weapons that the BSA might justifiably be allowed to use under various scenarios; and the reactions of NATO, the media, and the international community should commander BH C authorise release of an appropriate number of weapons. In the interim, however, we would very much appreciate your early initial views on this very difficult and potentially pressing problem." The first question I want to ask is: Here you reference a protocol to the weapons collection agreement that is attached to this document. Do you recall if you were present at the time the weapons collection agreement was negotiated and this protocol was discussed?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I was present in Sarajevo at the initiation period of negotiation between the Bosnian government and the Bosnian Serb party. After I saw that there was a distinct possibility of meeting of minds eventually on this issue, I departed from Sarajevo to meet with president of the Yugoslav republic in Belgrade and saw the -- all the details of the agreement between the two parties about Sarajevo had been put into detailed points only after my departure and the actual negotiation on the part of UNPROFOR was General David Rose, commander of our Bosnia and Herzegovina sector, but under the supervision of General de Lapresle from our headquarters in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time that this cable that we have in front of us was drafted and sent, was the release of weapons to the Serbs from weapon collection points seriously being considered to allow the Serbs to defend against these BiH attacks?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think from the Bosnian Serb viewpoint, all -- they had to prepare for all possible situations. I'm not sure whether, you know, it is possible to consider and put all the details in agreement of this kind, but I can understand why two parties may want to prepare themselves for all eventualities. But our concern was how to breach the differences between the two parties. Of course, from the Bosnian Serb viewpoint, the more weapons collection points there are, the better. And from Bosnian government side, the fewer these weapon collection points, the better. Because it will be easier to defend those points if there are only very few in number and it would facilitate monitoring and control of weapons collection points if they were fewer. But we had to eventually agree on the midway points to meet the two parties' concerns halfway.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn briefly to page -- I believe it's 4 of this document, we can look at the actual -- yes, it is. And we see before us a typed document which has at the top the fax header line that another witness identified as BH command forward command which was the UNPROFOR forward command in Sarajevo. And this is entitled: "Protocol of understanding between the civilian/military representatives of the Republika Srpska and UNPROFOR." Do you happen to know who drafted this document? Do you have any information as to that?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think General Michael Rose had a major hand on the UNPROFOR side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And at the time that you wrote this cable and forwarded this protocol, did you believe that this protocol reflected what had been agreed to with the Serb side in relation to weapon collection points?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I certainly hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now if we can look at P631, and again I have a hard copy for your convenience.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it would assist, the usher's assistance, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: For the -- if I just can interrupt you for a second. In the previous document we were talking about the NAC decision. NAC was an acronym for what? The parties have no disagreement on that? It came up a few times in court, both in the initial appearance -- Mr. Tieger, NAC, any idea? What your understanding is of NAC acronym. If the witness could tell us what NAC stands for. It's in the previous document. We don't have to stop now, but if the parties could just consider whether there's any agreement on what NA --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I can propose the Defence's view and see if that assists. I think it would mean the North Atlantic Council, a reference to a body that oversaw NATO. But I, unfortunately, don't have a copy of that document in front of me to be able to see the context of where it was used. I do know it is in a document but I can't remember precisely the formulation of how that was ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President, I just remember an earlier discussion during which the meaning of an acronym was resolved on the basis of an explicit reference in the document. I don't recall if this was the same -- okay. So presumably -- we'll take a look at whether surrounding documentation sheds direct light on the meaning or whether we're otherwise in a position to come to agreement on precisely what the acronym means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Akashi, if you could help us out to tell us what NAC stands for as an acronym in the previous document we looked at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Excellency, I'm unable to help in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you so much for at least --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think our military colleagues like to indulge in a lot of acronyms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it seems to be very popular in ... Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador, we have this document before us which is dated, I believe, 12th September 1994, again from you, going to several individuals in New York, again on weapon collection points. And the first page of this document appears to say that the protocol we just looked at was determined to be unsigned and invalid and it attaches the opinion of a legal advisor who I think -- from the next page his name might be Stefan Katz [phoen], but I don't know -- do you know if there was any legal advisor present for the negotiations with the Bosnian Serb side as to weapon collection points on the part of the UN?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: We had our legal advisor at UNPROFOR headquarters in Zagreb, certainly. But negotiation in this particular case was conducted in Sarajevo and in the case of Bosnian Serbs probably at Pale, and I don't think we had legal advisor as such, but there was a head of civil affairs which was Mr. Sergio De Mello.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. I just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us. And during this time-period, that is, September 1994, when this second cable was written, were there any discussions relating to the potential use of air power against the Serb side, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not offhand recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let's me see if we can look at D116 in e-court, and -- oh, I do have a hard copy of that as well which I can provide to the usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while we wait for the hard copy to reach you, from the version on the screen we can see that this is from General de Lapresle to Mr. Annan and Mr. Stoltenberg, dated 19 September 1994, with the subject of: "Sarajevo heavy weapons exclusion zone violation - 18 September." And if I can summarise portions of the same to ask a question. Here in part 1, we see the second sentence that says: "The BiH and BSA exchanged approximately 300 mortar rounds and 6.000 small-arm rounds. The attack was initiated by the BiH armija and was supported by mortars firing from residential areas within the city limits." And then it gives precise information as to parts from where they fired and where they fired upon. And then the bottom two lines -- two sentences, I should say, read: "These initial attacks were followed by a restrained BSA response using heavy weapons. Between 1807 and 1838 hours, the BSA retaliated from Poljine WCP (BP 910645) with 12 120-millimetre mortar rounds. The BSA mined access to the base plate to prevent FreBat 5 from" - and if we can go to the next page - "interfering. The BSA responded, targeting the Zetra stadium, the Presidency, the north area of the cathedral, and Sedrenik. The commander BHC called on both sides to immediately cease all military actions or he would be obliged to take all appropriate measures to protect the civilian population of Sarajevo including air-strikes. He also warned the BSA not to withdraw weapons from the weapon collection points. Copies of the commander's letters are attached." And the first question I have for you is: Do you recall if air-strikes were ever sought or requested against the Bosnian government side for their violation of the weapons exclusion zone?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not recall the instances of the kind you mentioned, Mr. Ivetic. But despite my clear instructions to differentiate air-strikes as distinct from close-air support, I'm afraid that some -- some of our military leaders rather used these two terms without discrimination. But at my level, at least, I always kept the differences in mind. Close-air support was an act of -- clearly an act of self-defence with very clear restraint. The NATO was asked to attack only the object which was in the process of hostile action with a view to killing UNPROFOR personnel or the weapons which they were using as self-defence means. While air-strike was a more political act in which we tried to send a message of restraint to either of the two parties, not to worsen the general situation which may hinder our objectives for humanitarian assistance or for general stabilisation of the situation. So that may not be my precise answer, but that's, I understood, as to what was an air-strike and what was CAS, close-air support action. But as I said, this distinction was not always kept in mind by the military people. But it was very important thing for us in order not to confuse or give unnecessary apprehensions particularly to the Bosnian Serb party but also to -- as a message to the Bosnian government side as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we look at item 2 on this document, we see that the author, General de Lapresle says: "The key facts are that the military action taken by both sides contravened UN S.C.R. 836, breached the 9 February 1994 airport agreement, and violated the 20-kilometre TEZ. The BiH initiated the attack and the BSA response was both defensive and restrained. The BSA did not withdraw weapons from the WCPs." Now, this is dated approximately -- the incident is six days after the memo we just looked at, the cable we just looked at which said that the protocol had not been signed and therefore has no legal standing. Did anyone inform the Serb side prior to this incident that the protocol we previously looked at was no longer considered valid by the UN?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Is that a question addressed to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I do not have a specific answer to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh, Your Honours, I see we're about one minute away from the break point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are. If you want to touch upon a new --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, I do. But I'm going to another document, so we might actually eclipse the one minute rather quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then take that -- use that one minute.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could look at 1D4654.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This is a rather lengthy document but one that you're well familiar with, sir. It is a book entitled: "In the Valley Between War and Peace," and it lists you -- I apologise the copy in e-court has a poor reproduction of the cover page so we can't see it. It's all black. But the first question I have for you: Is this book entirely authored by yourself?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then if we can turn to page 27 in e-court, it should correspond to pages 46 through 47 in the actual document, or the underlying book, I should say. It looks like we need the prior page in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And beginning on the bottom of the -- of page 46, you are talking about a situation where you say: "During the joint press conference after our discussion, Admiral Boorda and myself clearly stated that if NATO forces use air power in the Sarajevo region upon UN request, it will be used impartially against all the violators of cease-fire. This attitude, to maintain impartiality with regard to all three parties to the conflict (Serbs, Croats and Muslims), was in clear contrast to the subsequent NATO council decisions which targeted only Bosnian Serb forces as an enemy. The hard-headed and pragmatic approach of Admiral Boorda to air attack by NATO forces appeared to be in sharp contradiction to the approach advocated by the high leadership of the US administration, including President Bill Clinton." First of all, could you tell us who Admiral Boorda was? What was his function?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: He was the Force Commander of NATO southern command headquartered in Naples, Italy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I see we've eclipsed the break time by approximately one minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Mr. Akashi, we take a break again. We would like to see you back in 20 minutes. I again invite you to follow the usher. It's a little bit more than one minute, Mr. Ivetic. Therefore, we'll resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I announced already the time at which we will resume.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can the witness be escorted in the courtroom -- or is there one preliminary matter, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There is, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would it take?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I have two -- actually two. The first takes 15 seconds and the second takes a couple of minutes perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then we wait for the witness to be escorted in the courtroom. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The first one is quite simple and concerns the Court's inquiry about the acronym NAC. We agree with Mr. Ivetic that it refers to the North Atlantic Council. The second, Mr. President, is that the Court asked us to respond by today's date with respect to excerpts concerning the "Islamic Declaration," and I -- although sometimes we wait until end of the day to deal with those matters, I thought it was probably best to deal with it now so it didn't escape our attention. First of all, I wanted to clear up one quick -- or quickly clear up one apparent misconception about the tendering of the document, whether in its entirety or excerpts, and that is that somehow the impression, I think, was left that it was the Prosecution which was the moving force behind tendering the entirety of the document. That's not the case. We have never considered it to play a particularly significant role in this case. However, when it was proposed to us by the Defence that they tender the entirety of the document, we had no objection to that. Particularly in light of the various assertions reflecting the nature of the document, we considered that it would be fine if the Court could see the entirety and make its own assessment of what it was about. However, in light of the Court's preference and request, we have identified certain excerpts that go to both directly contextual issues that -- it is our submission that certain sentences or small portions have been misleadingly lifted from a larger paragraph or passage and also some selections that perhaps more broadly illustrate the tenor or nature of the document in the way that might be the case if the Court had the entirety. That said, we're also asking if it's not perhaps a -- at this point a bit more prudent and efficient to defer tendering of any further excerpts for the following reasons: Number one, there's at least one additional witness who we know raises the issue of the "Islamic Declaration." Number two, we've identified at least some discrepancies between the identified portions by the Defence and those that were referred to in court. And number 3, there still seems to be a translation in English issue that would benefit from some discussion. So if the Court agree with that, we'd asked that you defer it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we usually prefer to have already in evidence and then later perhaps replace new excerpts by the old ones. But perhaps here where there are a few other matters as well, especially that we are not yet at a point where we have, I would say, a clean English version, that means just a translation of what the B/C/S presents, under those circumstances -- and I see Mr. Stojanovic is not opposed to it, to -- to wait for a while, but not forget about it. That excerpts still are sought to be admitted and that we know later which excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
