utterances.text: Understood, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think you're a little bit over one hour and a half by now, so may I take it that you will conclude in the next session of one hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, sooner than the end of the last -- this session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, we just looked at a part of your book where you contrasted Admiral Boorda's approach with that advocated by the high leadership of the US, including President Bill Clinton. What was your understanding of the approach advocated by the American leadership and Mr. -- President Clinton?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I'd rather prefer not to comment on the highest political leadership of any -- any country.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you help us at least to identify in relation to -- in relation to Admiral Boorda's position, was it complementary or contrary to the position of the UN?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Here again I do not want to indulge in any speculation. But from my acquaintance with Admiral Boorda, I had highest the regard and very deep respect with regard to Admiral Boorda as a person, as an admiral, and he had a very astute understanding of human nature and nature of conflicts. So he was not just a soldier, but I thought he was a good statesman.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If we could turn to the next page in e-court, which should contain pages 48 and 49 of your book, I would propose to discuss with -- the last paragraph on page 48 which continues onto page 49, and it starts off: "On the same day ..." And I believe in reference to the prior paragraph it looks like we're talking about February 18. And you say here: "On the same day, I met with Karadzic in Pale where the headquarters of Bosnian Serb forces was situated, and also held discussions in Sarajevo with President Izetbegovic. In the meeting with Karadzic, we had to answer his questions on the definition and kinds of heavy weapons to be removed from the 20-kilometre exclusion zone. We also had to respond to the question: If Bosnian Serb forces were attacked by Bosnian government forces, would they be able to retrieve the weapons of the Serb side which had been placed under the control of the United Nations? On the number of collection sites, there was clear discrepancy between Karadzic, who wanted a maximum number for easy access, and the UN side, which desired a minimum number because of its troop limitation. However, we somehow managed to come to a mutually acceptable compromise." The first question I would ask is if this section accurately reflects the negotiations that were undertaken and the result.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I hope so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And where you say here that Karadzic wanted a maximum number of sites for easy access, was this in relation to retrieving weapons if attacked or something else?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we can turn to page 30 in e-court, which should correspond to pages 52 and 53 of your book -- I see again I'm one page off. If we could go to page 29 in e-court, that should now correlate to those pages. And again here at the bottom of the first page, the second-to-last paragraph reads as follows and it will bleed onto the top the next page, page 53: "On July 22nd, I talked with US Secretary of Defence William Perry who came to visit Zagreb. From his calm attitude and his readiness to listen to me, I had the impression that he was a sincere man. In our joint press conference after the meeting, he said that there was a meeting of minds between us on the use of force between NATO and UN sides, and it was agreed with the UN side that use of force should be robust but should be carried out prudently. "But I was startled to find out that in the statement of Defence Secretary Perry on his return to the United States, the phrase 'prudently' had been omitted and stress was put on taking robust measures against the Bosnian Serb forces. It was clear from the statement of President Bill Clinton himself that his posture was that there should be a clear distinction between good and evil, and that the good side, that is the Bosnian government, should be supported, and that the Bosnian Serb forces should be labelled as evil." The first question I want to ask you is: Apart from this instance, do you recall if there were any other instances when the agreed-to text was deviated - when I say "agreed to," between NATO and another party - was deviated from in subsequent announcements or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, just -- yeah, so there's no -- so the answer is clear and the question doesn't inadvertently expand it and I don't want to -- I would just suggest that the passage upon which this relies insofar as I read it doesn't necessarily -- doesn't refer to a specific text. It refers to some kind of consensus between the two people involved. So to -- so we've got an apples and oranges situation where this is now, I think, being incorrectly characterised as agreement on a specific text and now the witness is being asked to answer as if that were the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, does this cause you to rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then I'll wait for that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if there were other situations where language agreed to between the UN and another party was then presented differently or deviated from in subsequent pronouncements?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: From my limited experience of negotiations, these things have happened and do happen with -- yeah, with some frequency. So I think we should not generalise from specific instances.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in a general sense, do you stand behind what you have written in your book in this particular section?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. But my -- those passages should not be quoted out of context. I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will be glad to ... I guess, Your Honour, I would then perhaps take those chapters and extract them from the book and tender that as a reduced document, just the chapters in their entirety that these selections were taken from, to address --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it's a bit difficult for the Chamber at this moment to say: Do it this way or that way. I mean, context should be there. Whether that always requires the whole of a chapter, I do not know because I haven't read the book or the booklet as you called it, I think, in the Karadzic case. So therefore, I would invite, first of all, the parties to seek an agreement on what is such context that it would not mislead the Chamber in any way. And if do you not agree, well, then finally our problem is that we'd have to look at the whole book to see whether the excerpt is adequate. But could the parties first focus on it and try to resolve the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can. At least --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll -- the parties were the first, Mr. Akashi to take care that you're not quoted out of context. At the same time, as you may understand, this Chamber is not seeking to have large documents, even where contextualisation seems not to be necessary, to have that in evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate your judgement, which is very, very prudent, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Excellency, I have no further questions for you at this time. I thank you for your indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Akashi, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Tieger. Mr. Tieger is counsel for the Prosecution. You will find him not yet standing but now standing to your right. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you were asked during your examination-in-chief in the Karadzic case about whose interests it was to prolong the war longer than was inevitable or necessary. And I think there was some references to that today as well, and you were even directed to a portion of your book in respect of that question.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: A booklet, I prefer.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's -- that's modest of you, and I will comply with your request. In that connection, may I direct your attention to a meeting you had with Mr. Izetbegovic on the 2nd of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that's 65 ter 09621. If the Registrar could call that up, please. Sorry, that seems to be the wrong document. Sorry, Mr. Registrar, that would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this meeting held on the 2nd of February, Mr. Ambassador, looking at pages 1 and then going on to page 2 of the e-court, and on page 2 of the B/C/S, we can see a reflection of Mr. Izetbegovic's expression of distrust in the Geneva process. And he's recorded as stating: "The BiH government had to accept unwillingly the partition of the country based on ethnic division due to the pressure from the international community which had imposed the arms embargo without any recourse to the principles recognised by international law." And he went on to say that the Serb ethnic cleansing was not punished but rewarded, and continued that: "If the international community wants to create a Serb republic in Bosnia, they can do so only with the Serb municipalities, but the Serbs took 15 of our municipalities by force." I wanted to ask you, Mr. Ambassador, whether it was correct that the Bosnian government's attitude toward a permanent cease-fire reflected its concerns that that would cement or make permanent the results of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I think certainly, as you said, the concern and the preoccupation of the Bosnian government is that the acceptance of certain geographical delineation might lead to more permanent division of the country of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I remember Dr. Karadzic quoting from Robert Frost that somehow fences make or contribute to making good neighbours, so that was a general reflection of his philosophy that we have to recognise ethnic divisions. But in the circumstances in which there was much mingling of different ethnic or cultural groups, as in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I think it was some kind of physical, artificial attempt to create more divisions than necessary in a multi-ethnic country and society.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender that document, 09621.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7691, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ambassador, if I could ask you about one more related document or document related to the same issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If I could call up 65 ter 11148, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, this is a document stemming from an earlier period. It's a transcript of a portion of a tape of the 124th Bosnian Presidency Session held on the 20th of June, 1992. And on page 1 of the English, we -- and I think it's page 24 hard copy of the B/C/S, we can see General Halilovic discussing recent events in Bihac, noting that some kind of agreement reached on exchange and resettlement and urging the Presidency to take a stand, stating "because we're playing directly into the hands of those whose intention it is to create some ethnic territories, to move the population, and to create clean national units." And he continues on to describe a situation where people were given two to three hours to pack their personal belongings and leave. And then if we turn the page, going to page 3 in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can we have the B/C/S corresponding because it does not match what's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know how that anomaly occurred because ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. That would be -- I have this, according to Ms. Stewart, as page 26 in the B/C/S. I think the apparent discrepancy arises from the fact that the English pages are more limited than the B/C/S for some reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So now I'm on page 3 where Mr. Izetbegovic, I think under the heading "president," turns to the question that Halil asks --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Ms. Stewart tells me it's 28 in B/C/S I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: He notes that: The situation in Banja Luka is similar. They are threatened with destruction and told you can either move out and then we'll do an exchange. He continued: We can choose between either accepting this or not accepting this. If we don't accept it, then these people really can get hurt. If we accept it, we're legalising ethnic division, that is the alteration of the demographic picture of Bosnia, the creation of ethnically clean territories, like some precondition for the creation of some kind of Serbian state in Bosnia-Herzegovina. And on the next page, and I think on it's -- next page in English, please, and the same page in B/C/S, page 28, Mr. Izetbegovic notes: "Can we have peace at that price? No, we can't. Even if that were to happen, regarding all these agreements, I think they later simply point their cannons and kill all those people. Wherever they surrendered their weapons, et cetera, they ended up getting hurt." Mr. Ambassador, would this passage from a meeting in June of 1992 reflect another expression of the same concerns by the Bosnian leadership about the demographic impact and purpose of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: I should think so. And I can well appreciate the overriding concern about the so-called clear delineation along ethnic line of -- over a larger political entity, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank, you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd tender 65 ter 11148.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, should the B/C/S be the full version that's longer than the English or should it correspond to what's in English --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I certainly agree they should correspond. If there's a -- I'm not quite sure how that happened, but I think Mr. Ivetic's point is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Mr. Ivetic, you want to have the same excerpts in B/C/S as in English, only portions are translated --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, my -- well, my understanding is that the B/C/S is some 26 pages and the English is some five pages, so we have a lot that is not translated. If it is being entered into evidence, I thought --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would suggest the following, that Mr. Tieger makes an excerpt from the B/C/S version which corresponds with the English one. And if you want to add any portion, that you address Mr. Tieger so that he can include that in the new -- to be uploaded version, the same in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That would be perfectly acceptable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Registrar, let's reserve a number at this moment, because it's certainly not this document in its entirety. Or perhaps we could already do the English which is apparently the selection. Mr. Registrar, number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7692, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7692 is admitted into evidence, but the B/C/S version should again be uploaded and now in full accordance with the English translation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In connection with the questions raised during your examination-in-chief in the Karadzic case about the Muslims' alleged lack of interest in peace, you were also asked by Dr. Karadzic whether you remembered that "we," that is, the Bosnian Serb side, "have been ready to give up territory for peace, that we did not claim to keep all the territory that we controlled." And that's found at page 56 of D1361, the statement. In that connection, that is, the -- this issue of peace and giving up territory, may I first show you another document and then I will ask you further about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we call up, please, 65 ter 02393, e-court page 41 and B/C/S page 38. That's the 40th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. There we see Dr. Karadzic speaking to the members of the assembly and noting toward the bottom quarter of the page: "I guarantee that everything that extends the war is an attempt by the West to enable Muslims to bring territories back in order not to beg Serbs. But now the entire international community has to beg Serbs to give some territories back. So, we have to prepare ourselves to lose as little -- as less as possible in a firm, responsible, and statesman manner. But that we get the main part," and then he goes on. We also see above that, just above, Dr. Karadzic referring to some of the discussions and saying: "We did not say then how much of a percentage nor did we outline the borders but said we wanted to separate and strategic goals would be" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Too fast. "... and strategic goals would be territorial connection with the Drina river, Neretva river, sea, Sarajevo, Sava river, Una river, et cetera." And then we turn the page in English to page 42, still on the same page in B/C/S. Dr. Karadzic points out in respect of giving territory up, we -- for example, at the -- about the seventh or sixth line down: "We also cannot give that much at Nevesinje, we cannot give Srbobran, we cannot give town of Kupres. We are not willing to give right bank in Jajce ..." And then he continues just toward the bottom of that paragraph: "We have to keep strategic directions and quality of the country," and then just two lines down, another example of what can't be given up, "we have to keep Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, did Dr. Karadzic make -- tell you, as he explained in this passage of his speech to the Bosnian Serb Assembly, that it was his intention to give back as little as possible and only certain parts that did not conflict with the Bosnian Serb strategic objectives or other interests?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, with whom I had a lot of discussions on different occasions, conveyed to me the -- his principal concern is like what you quoted from him, from the Serb National Assembly. As you know, at one stage in the conflict, the Bosnian Serbs had at the maximum occasion about 70 per cent of the entire territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but in the end, the Bosnian Serb party at Dayton accepted the division of the country, about 49 per cent for themselves and 51 per cent to the Bosnian government side. So depending on at which stage of the conflict you consider the division as rational and acceptable would very much depend on the perspectives of two parties, or three parties, as -- as you may choose from, and I think the efforts -- a great deal of efforts were paid by UN and UN-associated mediators to take into account the principal concerns of the parties with as little as possible by way of exchange of territories. But I think this was a very difficult exercise and as I discussed the matter with people like Lord Owen, Stoltenberg and others, I think mediators made honest efforts to meet as many principal concerns as possible of the parties in the conflict, but this -- perhaps a perfect solution is the enemy of a good, reasonable solution, and I think that was the principal conclusions of the Dayton agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender those pages from the 40th. I presume -- I don't know -- I don't recall offhand if there is an ongoing selection from the 40th to add those to or if this will be the beginning of that, but either way I know that's the practice of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps Mr. Registrar could help us whether we had started already with the excerpting or whether this is -- then a number should be there already. If not, would you please assign a number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe it needs a number, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While verifying whether a number was already ever assigned, we provisionally now assign a new number. Mr. Registrar will verify whether portions had already been selected and admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the number will be P7693.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is reserved for the excerpt of this session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, you've made reference during the course of your testimony, both previously and today, to your effort to point out some of the either complexities or oversimplifications of the war in your booklet as seen by yourself and others with whom you shared an understanding. So, for example, we turn to page 38 of -- page 22 in e-court of your booklet, which is page 38 of the hard copy. That's 1D46 -- 1D04654. You point out that crimes were committed by all parties to the conflict, Muslim, Serb and Croat. I take it that's not a -- something you need to refer to your booklet to know that you mentioned. But it's correct, is it not, Mr. Ambassador, that that does not mean that there was no difference between the parties in terms of the quantum of crimes. And by way of example, as you note explicitly in your book, referring to comments by Lord Owen in that case, there was -- and I'm pointing -- I'm now at page 25 -- page 15 in the e-court, page 25 of the hard copy. There was "a quantum difference between the horrors perpetrated by them." And that's a correct reflection both of the -- of what you pointed out in your book and of the realities of the situation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: That's a very important point.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I believe at page 22 of your book, you also note - and that's under a chapter subheading entitled: "The madness of exclusive nationalism" - that in the situation of the former Yugoslavia, Bosnian Serb forces committed the most atrocious acts. Although you note that all sides were responsible for crimes and atrocities. And that's correct too?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you also point out in your book that this quantum difference reflected another difference and that one that General Rose cited and that you also cited in chapter one of your booklet. And that's found at page 16 of the e-court, page 26 of the hard copy: "Although all three sides were to some extent guilty of war crimes, genocide did not form part of official Bosnian government policy in the way that it clearly did with the Serbs." And that's also a point you made in your book and that reflected the reality as you understood it; correct?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'll be tendering those portions of the booklet but I'll wait until the end to amass them and work with the Defence as the Court noted earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we'll wait for the outcome of that conversation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now earlier today, Mr. Ambassador, you were asked some questions about the total exclusion zone and weapons retrieval. And specifically you were asked to compare the document you wrote in -- or the dispatch you sent in August of 1994, which is D112, that contained the protocol to the -- to P631 which is the document you sent on September 12th describing -- further describing your understanding of the -- of what had happened in connection with the protocol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I want to just call up P631 again very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm going to just remind you about the contents of about this because you were asked about it in the Karadzic case as well, and before I turn your attention to that passage I just wanted to bring this document to your attention again. Here, you note in your dispatch to Mr. Annan that: "The attached protocol is a Bosnian Serb proposal that was never accepted by us. The protocol was sent to us in error, and was forwarded to you without a full examination due to the urgency of the question at the time." He goes on to explain that the Bosnian Serbs had expressed concern during discussions in February and rather than entering into any written agreement, UNPROFOR noted their concerns and gave assurances that UNPROFOR units would be interpositioned between the two sides along the confrontation lines. The Bosnian Serb side nevertheless reserved its right to take adequate measures in case of an attack. "We did not endorse their position." It attaches also the legal advisor's comments contained on the following page, in particular point 4 of the following page, where it is pointed out: "From the available information, I have found that the protocol of understanding was a draft that had been prepared and submitted by the Bosnian Serb negotiators but was found unacceptable by the UNPROFOR negotiators and was never signed. Accordingly, it cannot be regarded as having any legal standing." And I point that out because you were asked about that in the Karadzic case but in your cross-examination and that can be found out --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If we can call up 65 ter number 33522, first to page 13, it's where the discussion begins. And you can see toward the bottom of the page beginning to describe -- discuss the document. If we can continue onto the next page. And next page, please. Go to the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me see at the very bottom of the page at 15, at 37755: "I'll ask you the question in a different way then. Dr. Karadzic in his comments yesterday asserted to that you this additional protocol, which he said provided or allowed the Serbs a right to remove heavy weapons from the weapons collection point in case of attack, was concluded, and that would" --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we go to the next page. I think it's on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I didn't realise. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "... was concluded, and that was agreement between UNPROFOR and the Bosnian Serbs. These two documents taken together, Mr. Ambassador," that means referring to the document you sent in August and the one we just looked at in September, "would tend to show that contrary to what Dr. Karadzic observed, this protocol was, in fact, never concluded; isn't that correct?" And you responded: "Yeah. I think copies of these messages I sent to New York headquarters seemed to endorse what you have concluded from it." I take it, Mr. Ambassador, that you stand by that position?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now in -- you were also asked by Dr. Karadzic during the course of the direct examination now in evidence about the assurances and representations of the Bosnian Serbs. By way of example, at page 22 of the e-court, Dr. Karadzic asked you to confirm that you always achieved something in Pale and never left with empty hands. Although you didn't confirm that. Or by way of another example, Dr. Karadzic pointed out alleged Bosnian Serb intentions to fully implement terms of agreement. And that can be found at page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do you want to show it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't think that will be necessary. This is a predicate to other matters and it's in evidence, so it's -- certainly if the witness would want some clarification, I'm happy to do so. But I -- I think for purposes of moving on to the next point that should be sufficient for him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to clear up, I think the transcript that we have on the screen where they have been going to the pages you cited is the cross-examination, so the numbers you're referencing are in relation to D13 -- 1561.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: 1361. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And apologies to the Registrar for not making clear that we moved from the document reflecting the cross-examination back to the 65 ter statement in evidence which is the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, Mr. Ambassador, I wanted to ask you this. In contrast to the suggestion that you could rely upon the representations made by Dr. Karadzic, it is correct, isn't it, as you stated in your booklet, at e-court page 43 - and that's, again, 1D4654, page 43 - that: "Karadzic as a negotiator had the tendency to twist the truth rather nonchalantly - a trait I observed not a few times." That's a correct reflection of what's in your booklet, sir, and of what you found to be the reality on the ground?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think you confirmed that in your testimony in the Karadzic case, and that's 65 ter 33522, page 19: "As I came to know these tendencies, I was, of course, made more cautious, and I became, as time went on, much more cautious." And that's at transcript 37759.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Lines 3 and 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that was in response to the question what kind of weight did you give to any undertakings, representations, or agreements entered into by Dr. Karadzic. And I take it you stand by that testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I do. I was particularly struck by this trait or characteristic of Dr. Karadzic not only during the negotiations in April 1994, but his response to my frequent requests for a visit to Banja Luka, he gave a promise to me and then later he sidetracked by raising one reason or another. And as a total consequence of that all, I never managed to visit Banja Luka during my tenure of duty in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me turn then to some of the discussions surrounding Gorazde, the representations that were made and the reflections of the reality on the ground, and also the efforts you made to visit Banja Luka and also contemporaneous indications of why you were trying to visit Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, that seems to be quite an area which might take quite some time. I'm looking at the clock to see whether we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that's a good suggestion, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But before we take that break, I've got -- first of all, I'd like to put on the record that Mr. Registrar informed me that the number P7693 which was reserved for the 40th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, that there's no excerpt yet there. So, therefore, that 65 ter 02393 will for the time being be attached to P7693 and is admitted. I further have a very short question for you, Mr. Akashi. You were earlier asked about the - let me take it literally - the quantum difference and you were asked, because you pointed at that in your book, whether that reflected the real situation. I think you confirmed that. I noted that in that page of your book, you're mainly quoting Lord Owen and General Rose. Do I understand your answer to be that you agree with Lord Owen and General Rose in respect of what is written in that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in that respect. But with regard to General Rose, I think he was not always accurate, although he was accurate most of the time, and I think General -- the Lord Owen was probably closer to my own evaluation of the situation than any of the military people did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the portions read to you which are quotes from others, you agree in that respect --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Having clarified this, we'll take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we continue, there are two matters which I'd briefly like to raise. Mr. Ivetic, witnesses later this week, I do understand that after this witness has concluded his evidence that we would continue with Mr. Kovac. But after that, that might not take up the whole week, up to and including Thursday. Any ...

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The witness that was originally scheduled to testify after the completion of General Kovac was unable to travel on that day and has thus been rescheduled. So we don't as of right now have any witnesses that can we could move up to that date given that most of the remaining witnesses are fixed either in relation to video-link or to their own schedules. And so that we right now after General Kovac finishing, which I think, given the remaining estimates, will probably take place on Wednesday, we'll probably be missing that last day, unfortunately, of the week, Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And this witness unable to travel, when was that known?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Last week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Last week. Okay. Try to do your utmost best. Then there's one other matter which is -- deals with the Rule 92 ter motion Djoko Razdoljac. And it will not take much time so I think slowly we could try already to get the witness in. On the 1st of September of last year, 2014, the Defence filed a 92 ter motion for Djoko Razdoljac. He is not on the Defence list, 19th of May, 2014, the Rule 65 ter witness list, as a result of the Chamber having instructed the Defence to remove him from an earlier version of its witness list. This was because Razdoljac's evidence had been admitted during Prosecution's case already. The Chamber addressed this issue during the Pre-Defence Conference at transcript page 20977 and advised the Defence how to proceed procedurally should it wish to have further evidence from this witness admitted. And under these circumstances, where this procedure has not been followed, the Chamber denies the Rule 92 ter motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the procedure implied seeking permission to do what you apparently did without asking permission. Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I had indicated to you just before we adjourned that I wanted to follow up on your testimony that you were particularly struck by the trait or characteristic of Dr. Karadzic to twist the truth, not only during the negotiations in April 1994 but also in respect of your frequent requests for a visit to Banja Luka. So I'd like to first turn to the -- to April 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we could call up 65 ter 10949, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: While this is coming up, Mr. Ambassador, I can tell you that this is an outgoing code cable from you to Mr. Annan, dated 7 April 1994, concerning meetings with Dr. Karadzic and President Izetbegovic. And if we turn to paragraph 3, we see that on the question of Gorazde you expressed the Security Council and your own deep concern over the current situation, and then it states: Although Dr. Karadzic has given me his assurances that the BSA, the Bosnian Serb army, will not attack Gorazde town and that General Rose may visit the enclave in the next few days, I stressed the importance of having accurate UNPROFOR information on what was happening in order to allay the fears of the international community and prevent the situation from reinforcing the negative image of the Bosnian Serb army. So I take it then that this is an accurate reflection of that portion of the meeting that took place on April 6th, 1994, in respect of the assurances that Dr. Karadzic gave you about Gorazde town?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now you also -- perhaps it's useful then to turn also to paragraph 12 on page 4 in which we see a reference to the other issue you mentioned just before the break, where your cable reflects the following: Turning then to the issue of ethnic cleansing and the violation of human rights in Banja Luka and the need to halt this practice, I suggested that I visit the area towards the end of next week. I further requested that UNPROFOR be permitted to increase its UNMO and civil affairs presence in the area and to install CIVPOL elements to reassure the population. Is it correct, Mr. Ambassador, that this is a reflection of the frequent requests by you to visit Banja Luka in response to the information you were receiving about ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Indeed, it is one such instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And just -- no. It's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7694, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we turn next, then, to 65 ter 03459.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 16th of April, 1994, again from you to Mr. Annan. And it contains a chronology of events mainly involving Gorazde for 15 April and 16 April 1994 as we see in the cover. If we turn to page 3, for example, which appears to reflect, as we see from the preceding page, events of the 15th of April, 1994. We see at 1920 Gorazde reported to be shelled again. Dr. Karadzic's response that it could be the Bosnians shelling themselves. If we then turn to page 4. At 2000 hours we see the reference to casualties arriving at Gorazde hospital for medical evaluation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Evacuation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I misspoke. Medical evacuation. And another example at page 5. At 1045, General Rose outlines the need to act if Serbs enter the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you're more than welcome to read the entirety of the document if it is necessary, Mr. Ambassador, and I just highlighted a few examples, but is it correct to say that this document reflects the fact that operations by the Bosnian Serb army were under way in the Gorazde area, prompting deep concerns by yourself and the international community? It's not necessary to characterise the entirety of the document or every --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Could we have the witness's answer verbally, please, for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think Judge Moloto noted what I noted which was you were nodding your head affirmatively. If you could answer verbally so it can be picked up by the transcript.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I have read and these paragraphs reflect the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And also the paragraphs which were read to you and which are not on our screen at this moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These are evolution of events in and around Gorazde in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 03459 will be Exhibit P7695, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7695 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Can we next turn to 65 ter 03460.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, as you can now see, this is another code cable from April from you to Mr. Annan, dated 17 April 1994, concerning the Gorazde crisis and, in particular, meetings with Dr. Karadzic and with President Izetbegovic. And it indicates immediately below that subject heading information concerning your meeting with Dr. Karadzic and with others present who are listed. And it reflects the following: "Despite the promises made by the Serbs last night on my preconditions for our meeting today, it turned out during the course of the day that most of the promises were not fulfilled: 1, none of the UN personnel had been released before the meeting, and only the Canadian soldiers and three UNMOs were released after my repeated request during the meeting; 2, even during the meeting, there was no cease-fire by the Bosnian Serb army which kept advancing to the edge of the town, and several rounds impacted in the town itself resulting in further civilian casualties; and 3, no concrete agreement was reached, thus no UNPROFOR troops were deployed in Gorazde today." Is that a reflection, Mr. Ambassador, of what you were describing in your testimony before the break; that is, the -- some of the reasons why you were struck during the Gorazde crisis by Dr. Karadzic's tendency or characteristic of twisting the truth?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes. I found repeatedly that his words and the situation on the ground in Gorazde did not correspond to each other. And I remember -- I'm not sure whether it was on this day or on a day before or right after this meeting with Dr. Karadzic, but Mr. Churkin, a special envoy of the Russian Federation who accompanied me in one of the negotiations, decided to leave the meeting in total disgust and he decided to go back to Sarajevo and he did not return. But contrary to the advice of some of my associates who remained with me at Pale, I was very patient. I wanted to follow up on the progress of the return of UNPROFOR captives, and either no progress or extremely limited progress was registered. And Churkin did not want to stay with Karadzic for the press conference. He had left. But in order to save Karadzic's face, I decided to stay for the joint press conference, but at -- upon -- after the press conference, Karadzic invited me to stay for dinner. I said I do not want to stay for dinner, and he should understand my reasons. My reason was my total disgust with the lack of progress and the discrepancy between his words and progress on the ground. And I also remember I was negotiating with Karadzic in Geneva on Gorazde, and -- but there, again, the progress was extremely slow or almost nil, so I decided to leave Geneva to go back to my headquarters in Gorazde. I did it in a somewhat dramatic way so that Karadzic should know that -- my disillusionment with negotiations. And finally when I was checking out from the Hotel Intercontinental, Karadzic sent for me and asked for urgent meeting in which I decided to go back to the hotel, and -- but here again, I checked everything he promised. I checked it with our troops and UNMOs on the ground again, and still there were frequently discrepancies. So the -- the progress was finally registered when we met with President Milosevic in Belgrade, and there I accepted to negotiate with Karadzic, and General Mladic was there, and we negotiated with each other for more than 11 hours. Finally, I -- upon my proposal to have a smaller restricted meeting, including Milosevic, Karadzic, and General Mladic on their side, and General de Lapresle and myself on the UN side, I -- I referred to imminence of NATO air-strike - air-strike as distinct from close-air support - and I appealed to them to heed these indications which were real. And I appealed to their sense of history of the Serb people, proud people with a glorious history. And I told them that, you know, they are faced with a crucial choice and their judgement in -- you know, vis-à-vis their history was at stake. And Milosevic immediately understood the vital importance of the occasion and the imminence of a decision, but Karadzic and Mladic had still difficulties. But, in the end, they had to come around. And we reached a final agreement towards midnight, and the next morning we came back to examine the text of the agreement. And Karadzic still made some points, technical points. General Mladic, once he got satisfaction on the main points from his viewpoint, he was not -- he did not, you know, need any more examination of the text. And we signed the crucial document. And when I left the Presidency in Belgrade, I looked at my watch. I know it was 20 minutes to midday, and my deadline was midday. So I was very moved that, here again, after Sarajevo crisis in February 1994, here again in Gorazde in April 1994 we were able to avoid the catastrophe of a massive air-strike by NATO through means of diplomacy. Yeah. So these describe these events.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7696, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7696 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, I note that in paragraph 2 of your cable for the April 17th meeting it refers to the fact that the Serbs insisted that the right bank of Drina river is their territory and that was their basis for certain of the positions they took. In that connection, if I could also turn you to 65 ter 13405. This is a document also dated the 17th of April from Mr. Andreev to Mr. De Mello. Also concerning so -- it begins by saying: "The fate of Gorazde appears now to be the hands of the Bosnian Serb forces. Serb forces have taken all high ground to the north of the town and have reached the river to the south. They are within a kilometre or two of the town centre in all directions. "When we left Pale today, we had only the most limited of oral agreements." It lists some of those, including immediate cease-fire, withdrawal of forces, maximum restraint, limited medical evacuation, and release of all remaining UN hostages. And if we turn to the next page --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Paragraph 3, it states: "In retrospect, it is clear that the Serbs have used their negotiations with the United Nations as a cover for the prosecution of their offensive." And it explains that in more detail. It concludes by saying: "Attacks continued during our presence in Pale." Paragraph 4 notes that: "No real progress was made today," and notes in the middle of that paragraph, Dr. Karadzic insisted that "the right bank of the Drina will be ours." Mr. Akashi, does that conform with your recollection of the circumstances at the time and is that another reflection --

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Yes. It's only now that the French translation has finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think we are caught up now, Mr. Akashi. And I had asked you whether that conformed with your recollection of events at the time and was it another reflection of the discrepancies between what you were told and what was happening on the ground?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I would say certainly it was so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would tender that document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7697, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7697 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me change directions slightly and show you a document that -- not emanating from you, Mr. Ambassador, but from the Bosnian Serb army; that's P5039.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, while waiting for the document, would you please keep in mind that we want to finish at 15 minutes past 2.00 sharp today.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 17th of April titled: "Very urgent," comes from the Chief of Staff of the VRS Main Staff, General Milovanovic. And it reflects that it -- on the 17th of April at 2055 hours the president of Republika Srpska ordered, and if we look at -- so number 1, we see an order to now stop the fire by artillery and mortars into the city of Gorazde. And number 2, within the 3-kilometre radius on the right bank of the Drina river capture all features and in particular the urban parts of the city, and then withdraw the heavy weaponry outside the zone of the 3-kilometre radius. Dig it in and camouflage it. And with respect to the left bank as reflected in item 3, to take up favourable positions so that the whole zone is encircled by the Army of Republika Srpska. Is that consistent with the information you were receiving at the time from the -- from your sources on the ground and inconsistent with the representations you were receiving from Dr. Karadzic? That is, number one, that in fact artillery and mortars had apparently been fired into Gorazde town; number 2, contrary to his representation on April 7th, that the Army of Republika Srpska was engaged in the attack on Gorazde town?

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, it corresponds to my memory of the situation as we saw from UN side.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And finally, I think I can conclude if we call up 65 ter 16806. That may be a document that is now in evidence as D1362.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's an outgoing cable from you to Mr. Annan on the 23rd of April, 1994, reflecting information from your meetings with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic. You were asked in your examination-in-chief this morning about a certain portion of this document but I want to direct your attention to another portion and that is paragraph 4 on page 3. There, you're addressing the critical need to resolve the crisis. You state in the middle of the page -- you also refer to NATO could take decisions which could have tragic repercussions all around. You state that there should be no illusions on any side of the seriousness of the present situation and of the international community's revulsion towards it. And you note that it was a tragedy, a human and humanitarian tragedy out of proportion to any provocation that the Bosnian Serb army may have initially had from the BiH. And then you referred to the unacceptably high civilian casualties of just the previous day, almost 100.

utterances.speaker: YASUSHI AKASHI
utterances.text: Yes, I did my very best, I recollect, to make the Bosnian Serb side, its leadership to be fully aware of the consequences of their action around Gorazde. It was very clear from this that they were using Gorazde in order to improve their general situation throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. But they went so far with regard to Gorazde issue that they were going out of their way, out of achieving immediate objective in Gorazde, and I gave the most frank warnings in that regard. And this corresponds to what I said earlier today with -- at the meeting with President Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's now 2.15. We have to conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Akashi, we'll conclude for the day and we'll adjourn until tomorrow morning, 9.30. We all expect that tomorrow morning that we'll be able to conclude hearing your evidence. Meanwhile, I instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, whether that's testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. If that is clear to you, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you very much, Excellency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day, and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday, the 24th of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.
